[NSTG.9.1] **The seed is the read-back half of write-through persistence.** The
`ds_engine_cache_callbacks` write-through hooks ([NSTG.2.1.1], [LSTO.4.5.2])
mirror each `cache` write to a durable store so it survives a restart; they do
**not** read anything back. On the next startup the integrator restores the
saved entries into the fresh engine's cache with `ds_engine_cache_seed`
([IARC.12]) — one call per persisted `key` → `value`, before the engine's first
stream event ([NLFC.9.1]). The two are a matched pair: `set_cb` / `delete_cb` persist outward,
the seed hydrates inward.

Because they are a pair, every delete notification is one to act on: both
reasons the callback can carry — the verb and TTL expiry ([NSTG.2.4]) — mean
the value is genuinely finished, so the store drops the row in each case and
the seed has nothing it should have restored.

That is only true because a cache write past its cap **fails** rather than
evicting ([LSTO.4.7.5]). Were it otherwise there would be a third reason meaning
*still valid, could not hold it*, and a store acting on it would destroy under
memory pressure precisely what the durable copy existed to survive.
